content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its recommendations for treating children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These updates also address simplified service delivery and diagnostics for HCV. The recommendations are based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of available evidence, which evaluated the efficacy and safety of direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) in this population. HCV is a significant global cause of liver disease, leading to substantial morbidity and mortality. In 2019, WHO estimated that approximately 58 million people were living with HCV, with 399,000 deaths attributed to the infection. The introduction of short-course, oral, curative DAA regimens in 2013 revolutionized HCV treatment. These regimens are highly effective, have excellent safety profiles, and require shorter treatment durations compared to older interferon-based therapies. The primary goal of HCV treatment is to prevent advanced liver disease and extrahepatic complications by eliminating active infection (viremia). Additionally, treatment reduces the risk of transmission and improves patients' quality of life. Since 2017, DAAs have been approved for use in adolescents aged 12 years and older, and more recently, for younger children. The first DAA regimen approved for younger children was the fixed-dose combination of sofosbuvir and ledipasvir (SOF + LDV). Other approved regimens include sofosbuvir and ribavirin (SOF + RBV) for children aged 3–17 years with HCV genotypes 2 and 3, and glecaprevir and pibrentasvir (GLC + PIB), a pangenotypic regimen approved for children as young as three years. Sofosbuvir and velpatasvir (SOF + VEL), another pangenotypic regimen, was approved in 2020 for children aged six years and older, and in 2021 for children aged three years and older. Additionally, the combination of sofosbuvir, velpatasvir, and voxilaprevir (SOF + VEL + VOX) was approved in 2021 for adolescents aged 12–17 years. The combination of sofosbuvir and daclatasvir (SOF + DCV) has also been widely used in observational studies, demonstrating safety and efficacy, although it has not been submitted for regulatory approval. A systematic review conducted in 2020 identified 39 eligible clinical trials and observational studies involving 1,796 children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection. The pooled data showed a 100% sustained virological response at 12 weeks post-treatment (SVR12) among those who completed treatment. Headache and fatigue were the most commonly reported adverse events, while serious adverse events were rare. The updated recommendations aim to provide evidence-based guidance on the use of DAAs for children and adolescents with chronic HCV infection. The review focused on three key questions: (1) which DAA regimens should be used for adolescents aged 12–18 years, (2) which regimens should be used for children aged 6–11 years, and (3) which regimens should be used for children aged 3–5 years. The analysis included randomized clinical trials, non-randomized comparative studies, and observational studies. The review found that DAA regimens are highly effective across all age groups, with SVR12 rates consistently exceeding 96%. The evidence supports the use of pangenotypic regimens such as SOF + VEL and GLC + PIB for children and adolescents, as well as SOF + LDV for specific genotypes. The safety profile of these regimens is excellent, with low rates of treatment discontinuation and minimal adverse events. The WHO emphasizes the importance of expanding access to DAAs for children and adolescents, particularly in lowand middle-income countries where the burden of HCV is highest. Simplified service delivery models and improved diagnostics are critical to achieving this goal. The updated recommendations provide a framework for scaling up HCV testing and treatment in this vulnerable population, with the ultimate aim of eliminating HCV as a public health threat.
